headings.title: Introduction and Definition of Hypertension
headings.content: Hypertension, commonly known as high blood pressure, is a chronic cardiovascular condition in which the systemic arterial blood pressure is persistently elevated. For nursing students preparing for clinical practice, it is vital to understand that blood pressure is determined by two main physiological factors: cardiac output and total peripheral resistance. When these variables increase—due to factors such as increased blood volume, increased heart rate, or vasoconstriction—the pressure exerted against the arterial walls rises. Clinically, a diagnosis of hypertension is rarely made on a single reading; instead, it requires sustained elevated blood pressure measurements over multiple healthcare visits. In the context of nursing care in Nigeria, understanding this definition forms the foundation for proper patient assessment, health education, and the prevention of long-term end-organ damage. Uncontrolled hypertension places a massive strain on the heart, kidneys, brain, and vasculature, earning it the clinical moniker of the 'silent killer' because many individuals remain asymptomatic for years while progressive internal damage occurs.

headings.title: Epidemiology and Public Health Significance in Nigeria
headings.content: Hypertension is a major public health challenge globally and represents a rapidly growing epidemic in Nigeria and across sub-Saharan Africa. Epidemiological data indicates a rising prevalence of high blood pressure among both urban and rural Nigerian populations, driven by ongoing epidemiological transitions, rapid urbanization, adoption of Western lifestyles, dietary shifts toward processed foods high in sodium, and increasing levels of chronic stress. This high prevalence places a heavy burden on the already fragile Nigerian healthcare infrastructure, as cardiovascular complications lead to high rates of morbidity, premature mortality, and hospitalization. For nursing students, recognizing the public health significance of hypertension means looking beyond individual hospital beds to understand community-level determinants of health. Public health nursing strategies in Nigeria must focus on large-scale educational campaigns, lifestyle modification programs, and decentralized screening initiatives to reach vulnerable populations who may lack regular access to primary healthcare services. Addressing this epidemic requires coordinated efforts from nurses, community leaders, and policymakers to mitigate risk factors and improve early detection across all geopolitical zones of the country.

headings.title: Pathophysiology and Underlying Risk Factors
headings.content: The pathophysiology of primary (essential) hypertension is multifactorial and involves complex interactions between genetic, environmental, and neurohumoral factors. Key mechanisms include overactivity of the sympathetic nervous system, dysfunction of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS), renal sodium handling abnormalities, and endothelial dysfunction leading to increased vascular tone and remodeling. Secondary hypertension, which accounts for a smaller percentage of cases, results from an identifiable underlying pathology such as renal parenchymal disease, renovascular stenosis, primary aldosteronism, or pheochromocytoma. Underlying risk factors are broadly categorized into non-modifiable and modifiable factors. Non-modifiable risk factors include advancing age, family history of hypertension, male gender, and genetic predisposition. Modifiable risk factors—which form the primary target for nursing interventions—include unhealthy diet (high sodium, low potassium), physical inactivity, obesity (especially central adiposity), excessive alcohol consumption, tobacco use, and chronic psychosocial stress. Understanding these pathways enables nursing students to connect a patient's clinical presentation and lifestyle history directly to their elevated blood pressure readings, guiding effective, individualized care plans.

headings.title: Classification and Blood Pressure Categories
headings.content: Accurate classification of blood pressure is essential for guiding clinical diagnosis, risk stratification, and therapeutic management. Standard guidelines categorize blood pressure into distinct categories based on systolic blood pressure (SBP) and diastolic blood pressure (DBP) measurements taken in a clinical setting. Normal blood pressure is generally defined as less than 120/80 mmHg. Elevated blood pressure ranges from an SBP of 120-129 mmHg and a DBP of less than 80 mmHg. Stage 1 hypertension is diagnosed when SBP is between 130-139 mmHg or DBP is between 80-89 mmHg. Stage 2 hypertension represents a more severe elevation, characterized by an SBP of 140 mmHg or higher, or a DBP of 90 mmHg or higher. Furthermore, when measurements exceed 180/120 mmHg, it constitutes a hypertensive emergency or urgency depending on the presence of acute target organ damage. For nursing students, mastering these numerical thresholds is critical because they dictate whether a patient requires lifestyle counseling alone or immediate initiation of antihypertensive drug therapy, as well as helping to identify patients at risk for cardiovascular events.

headings.title: Clinical Manifestations and Assessment Techniques
headings.content: While hypertension is often asymptomatic, thorough clinical assessment by the nurse is vital for identifying potential signs of end-organ damage or secondary causes. When symptoms do occur—typically in severe hypertension or during crises—they may include occipital headaches (often worse in the morning), dizziness, palpitations, fatigue, blurred vision, epistaxis, and shortness of breath upon exertion. Comprehensive assessment techniques begin with proper measurement of blood pressure using a calibrated sphygmomanometer and an appropriately sized cuff. The patient should be seated quietly for at least five minutes with feet flat on the floor and arm supported at heart level; caffeine, exercise, and smoking should be avoided prior to measurement. Nurses must also conduct a focused physical examination, assessing peripheral pulses, auscultating for carotid or renal bruits, checking for fundoscopic abnormalities in the retina, and palpating for point of maximal impulse (PMI) displacement which indicates left ventricular hypertrophy. Laboratory and diagnostic investigations ordered in conjunction with clinical findings include urinalysis for protein, serum electrolyte panels, fasting blood glucose, lipid profiles, and electrocardiograms (ECG) to evaluate electrical and structural heart status.

headings.title: Community-Based Screening and Early Detection
headings.content: Community-based screening is a cornerstone of secondary prevention, particularly in resource-limited settings like Nigeria where many individuals lack regular contact with primary care facilities. Nurse-led screening programs take healthcare services directly to community gathering places such as markets, churches, mosques, workplaces, and community town halls. These initiatives enable early detection of undiagnosed hypertension, significantly reducing the incidence of stroke, myocardial infarction, and chronic kidney disease. During community outreaches, student nurses play an active role by measuring blood pressure correctly, documenting readings accurately, and offering basic triage. Crucially, community screening must be accompanied by immediate health counseling and structured referral pathways. A single elevated reading in a noisy market setting does not constitute a definitive diagnosis; therefore, nurses must educate clients on the importance of confirmatory follow-up at a primary health center. Furthermore, community screening empowers citizens by raising health awareness, fostering health-seeking behaviors, and addressing cultural misconceptions regarding chronic non-communicable diseases in Nigeria.

headings.title: Pharmacological and Non-Pharmacological Management
headings.content: The management of hypertension involves a combination of non-pharmacological lifestyle modifications and pharmacological interventions tailored to the patient's cardiovascular risk profile. Non-pharmacological management is the first line of defense and should be recommended to all patients, regardless of whether drug therapy is required. Key lifestyle changes include dietary sodium restriction (such as reducing reliance on heavily salted local seasonings), adopting the Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension (DASH) eating plan rich in fruits, vegetables, and low-fat dairy, engaging in regular aerobic exercise (e.g., brisk walking for at least 30 minutes most days of the week), achieving and maintaining a healthy body weight, moderating alcohol intake, and completely avoiding tobacco products. When lifestyle modifications alone fail to achieve target blood pressure goals—or immediately in patients with Stage 2 hypertension or high cardiovascular risk—pharmacological therapy is initiated. Commonly prescribed classes of antihypertensive medications include thiazide diuretics, calcium channel blockers (CCBs), angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors, and angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs). Nursing responsibilities include monitoring for drug side effects (such as dry cough with ACE inhibitors or electrolyte imbalances with diuretics), assessing medication adherence, and educating patients on the necessity of lifelong compliance.

headings.title: Complications and Crisis Intervention
headings.content: Long-term, uncontrolled hypertension exacts a severe toll on the body, leading to critical target organ damage and life-threatening crises. Chronic complications affect major vascular beds: in the brain, hypertension is the leading cause of stroke (both ischemic and hemorrhagic); in the heart, it leads to left ventricular hypertrophy, heart failure, and coronary artery disease; in the kidneys, it causes nephrosclerosis and chronic kidney disease potentially progressing to end-stage renal disease; and in the eyes, it causes hypertensive retinopathy. A hypertensive crisis represents an acute, severe elevation of blood pressure and is subdivided into urgency and emergency. A hypertensive urgency involves blood pressure exceeding 180/120 mmHg without acute evidence of target organ damage; this is managed by gradually lowering blood pressure over 24 to 48 hours using oral medications. Conversely, a hypertensive emergency involves blood pressure above 180/120 mmHg accompanied by acute, ongoing target organ damage—such as encephalopathy, acute myocardial infarction, unstable angina, pulmonary edema, or aortic dissection. Hypertensive emergencies require immediate hospitalization in an intensive care unit (ICU) and administration of continuous intravenous antihypertensive agents with rapid, controlled blood pressure reduction to prevent permanent disability or death.

headings.title: Role of the Community Health Nurse in Prevention and Patient Education
headings.content: The community health nurse plays a pivotal, multifaceted role in the prevention, early detection, and ongoing management of hypertension within Nigerian communities. Operating at the primary healthcare level, nurses act as educators, advocates, clinicians, and counselors. Patient education is paramount; nurses must empower patients and their families with culturally sensitive knowledge regarding the disease process, the dangers of non-adherence, the importance of balanced local nutrition, and the necessity of regular blood pressure monitoring. Community health nurses also conduct home visits to assess the home environment, evaluate family support systems, and check medication adherence among elderly or immobile clients. Furthermore, nurses bridge the gap between community members and the formal healthcare delivery system by facilitating smooth referral networks, organizing support groups for hypertensive patients to share coping strategies, and engaging in health advocacy with local leaders to promote healthy public policies, such as smoke-free public spaces and community walking paths. By fulfilling these roles, nurses significantly reduce the burden of hypertension and improve overall population health outcomes in Nigeria.
